body.hook: Push a wall as hard as you like and you do no work on it, yet carrying a bag along a flat corridor does none either. Why?

overview.why: Work is the bridge between forces and energy, so it lets you solve motion problems without tracking time or acceleration. In the exam it appears in energy, power and efficiency questions; outside it, it explains why engines, cyclists and lifts need fuel.
learn: Calculate the work done by a constant force using W = Fs cos θ
Relate the work done by the resultant force to the change in kinetic energy
Apply conservation of mechanical energy with Ek, gravitational and elastic potential energy
Calculate power using P = Fv and efficiency from energy or power
Interpret a force-displacement graph as work done

frames.title: Work is energy transferred
frames.text: When a force moves an object through a displacement, energy is transferred to or from it. This transfer is called work done. Work is measured in joules (J), and it is a scalar quantity.

frames.title: Think of it like pushing a shopping trolley
frames.text: Pushing a trolley along an aisle, your effort turns into the trolley's motion. Pushing at an angle wastes some effort pressing it into the floor. Only the part of your push along the way it moves counts as work.

frames.title: Work done by a constant force
frames.text: Only the component of force along the displacement does work.

frames.title: Force at an angle
frames.text: A block is pulled along the ground by a force at 30° above the horizontal. Only the horizontal component F cos 30° does work along the displacement.

figure.alt: A block on a horizontal surface with a pulling force directed up and to the right at 30 degrees above the horizontal, weight acting downwards and normal force acting upwards.

data.prompt: A force of 10 N acts at 90° to the displacement of an object. How much work does it do?

options.why: Work is not per metre; this ignores cos 90°.
Work is negative only if the force has a component opposite to the displacement.

options.text: Cannot be found without the displacement
options.why: cos 90° = 0, so the work is zero whatever the displacement.

data.right: Correct: cos 90° = 0, so no energy is transferred.
data.wrong: W = Fs cos θ, and cos 90° = 0.

frames.title: Sign of work
frames.text: Work is positive when the force has a component along the displacement (energy transferred to the object), and negative when it opposes it, as friction does (energy removed from the object).

data.problem: A rope pulls a crate 12 m along a horizontal floor with a force of 50 N at 40° above the horizontal. Calculate the work done by the rope.

data.wrong: Use θ as the angle between the force and the vertical or the surface normal.
data.right: θ is the angle between the force direction and the displacement direction.
data.why: Using the wrong angle gives sin instead of cos, and the wrong work.

data.prompt: A 20 N force acts at 60° to the direction a trolley moves, which is 5.0 m. Calculate the work done by the force.
data.wrong: Use W = Fs cos θ with cos 60° = 0.5. Using the full 100 J ignores the angle.

frames.title: Work and kinetic energy
frames.text: The work done by the resultant force on a system equals the change in its energy. For a body being accelerated, this is the change in kinetic energy: W = ΔEk.

frames.title: Conservation of mechanical energy
frames.text: Mechanical energy is Ek + gravitational Ep + elastic Ep. With no friction or resistive forces it is conserved, and work is the energy transformed between these forms. Non-conservative forces change the total by the work they do.

data.problem: A 0.50 kg ball is dropped from rest from a height of 4.0 m. Ignoring air resistance, determine its speed just before landing. Use g = 9.81 N kg^-1.
steps: Loss of Ep = gain of Ek

data.prompt: Sort these by whether they are included in mechanical energy or are not.
data.right: Mechanical energy is only Ek + gravitational Ep + elastic Ep.
data.wrong: Mechanical energy is the sum of kinetic, gravitational potential and elastic potential energy only.

frames.title: Power and efficiency
frames.text: Power is the rate of energy transfer. For a force moving an object at constant velocity along the force, P = Fv.

data.prompt: A car moves at a constant 20 m s^-1 against a total resistive force of 600 N. Calculate the useful power the engine delivers.
data.right: Constant speed means driving force = 600 N, so P = Fv = 600 × 20 = 12 000 W.
data.wrong: At constant speed the driving force equals the resistive force; then P = Fv.

data.statement: A satellite in a circular orbit has the gravitational force on it doing no work, because the force is always perpendicular to its velocity.
data.right: Yes: θ = 90° so W = 0 and its kinetic energy stays constant.
data.wrong: The force points to the centre and the motion is along the tangent, so θ = 90° and cos θ = 0.

cards.front: Work done by a constant force

cards.back: Equals the change in kinetic energy
Useful output / total input (energy or power)

key_terms.definition: The energy transferred by a force moving an object through a displacement; W = Fs cos θ.
The work done when a force of 1 N moves an object 1 m in the direction of the force.
Energy a body has due to its motion; ½mv².
Energy due to position in a gravitational field; ΔEp = mgΔh near Earth's surface.
Energy stored in a stretched or compressed spring; ½k(Δx)².
The sum of kinetic, gravitational potential and elastic potential energy.
The rate of doing work or transferring energy; P = ΔW/Δt = Fv.
The ratio of useful work or power output to total work or power input.

outcomes.statement: Calculate the work done by a constant force acting at an angle to the displacement.

check.prompt: A force of 30 N acts at 30° to a displacement of 4.0 m. Calculate the work done, in J, to 2 significant figures.
check.wrong: Use W = Fs cos θ with cos 30° = 0.866.

outcomes.statement: State the relationship between the work done by the resultant force and kinetic energy.

check.prompt: The resultant force on a body does 40 J of work on it. What is the change in the body's kinetic energy?

options.why: This wrongly halves the work, confusing it with ½mv².
Non-zero resultant work changes the kinetic energy.

check.wrong: Work by the resultant force equals the change in kinetic energy.

outcomes.statement: Determine the speed of an object using conservation of mechanical energy.

check.prompt: A frictionless roller coaster car starts from rest at a height of 5.0 m. Determine its speed at ground level. Use g = 9.81 N kg^-1.
check.wrong: Equate mgh to ½mv², so v = √(2gh); the mass cancels.

outcomes.statement: Calculate the efficiency of a device from its energy input and useful output.

check.prompt: A motor takes in 500 J of electrical energy and lifts a load, gaining 350 J of gravitational potential energy. Calculate its efficiency as a decimal.
